articles.headline: Freshman Gridder Dies Of Self Inflicted Gunshot Wound
articles.author: David Erlewine
articles.body:
Family, friends, and the Ohio Wesleyan community mourned the death of freshman Trevor Howard Hartley, who committed suicide Wednesday, Jan. 12.

Hartley, 19, of 2975 Brandon Road, Upper Arlington, a suburb of Columbus, died of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, said Upper Arlington Police Detective Ernie Ankrom.

Hartley, a resident of 113 Thomson Hall, played fullback for the Bishops football team.

He apparently shot himself in the head with a 9mm handgun while sitting in his car at the Kingsdale Shopping Center in Upper Arlington, Ankrom said.

Freshman Alicia Heins, Hartley's girlfriend, said Hartley was in her room until 8:10 p.m. Wednesday night.

She said they were discussing their relationship before Hartley left. Hartley said "he was leaving the world because there is too much hate in the world and people trying to hurt each other."

Heins went down the hall and got sophomore Steve Jauffrineau, and he ran after Hartley. Jauffrineau said he caught up to Hartley at his car.

Hartley told Jauffrineau he was leaving this world because there is too much hate and people trying to hurt each other." Then Hartley drove off, he said.

Hartley called Heins at about 8:50 p.m. and said he had his brother's gun and was going to the Upper Arlington High School football stadium, Heins said.

Heins called the Upper Arlington police and 911. The Upper Arlington police told Heins to call the Delaware Police and she did. They sent a police officer over to speak to her.

Ankrom said Upper Arlington police dispatched three cruisers to the stadium at about 9:07 p.m. but found it locked and didn't find Hartley. Since Hartley's parent's home was nearby, the cruisers searched the area around his house.

Hartley's body was found at 9:52 p.m. after some Big Bear employees in the Kingsdale shopping center called police about a man slumped over in his car.

Upper Arlington Police Detective Jim Rothwell processed the police report and said he knew Hartley and was shocked by what had happened.

Rothwell said Hartley volunteered for the Upper Arlington Police and Medic departments. He added that Hartley was always helpful.

A part-time associate with Grant Medical Center and Ohio State University golf course, people remembered Hartley for his hard work and enthusiasm.

Upper Arlington firefighter Mike Cooper said Hartley was an enthusiastic worker who got along well with everyone.

Rothwell said everyone at the station knew Hartley.

Heins denied rumors that Hartley was distraught over a break-up with her which contributed to his suicide. "We never broke up," she said.

She added that earlier that day "we were discussing our relationship."

James Hartley, Trevor's father, said, "They did not break up." Trevor's problems were much deeper than that," he said.

"Often, Trevor would tell me, 'Dad, it's not a nice world." said J. Hartley. "He obviously knew and cared much more about what was going on in the world than I realized.

"Trevor tried to do a lot for many people, "J. Hartley said. As counselors have said, he wanted to help people. He was able to assist the medics, police, and the hospital.

articles.headline: Anderson Loses Battle With Cancer
articles.author: Bob West
articles.body:
Dr. Daniel E. Anderson, professor of philosophy and one of the most popular professors at Ohio Wesleyan, died yesterday after a lengthy battle with cancer.

Anderson, known as 'Andy' to many of his colleagues and friends, was chairman of the philosophy department he has taught at since 1964.

Anderson taught at Washington and Jefferson College and the University of New Orleans before joining the faculty here in Delaware.

He was diagnosed as having cancer in his lower back last spring, but remained in the classroom up until late this fall, when the his health required he give up teaching.

His health continued to worsen, forcing Anderson to enter the hospital the first week in January. He entered a coma last Thursday, and remained in that state until his death Tuesday afternoon.

Anderson will be remembered by many for the relaxed attitude, both in and out of the classroom, that constantly attracted students to him and his unique position strongly supporting the women's movement in society.

Loyd Easton, philosophy professor-emeritus from OWU, credited Anderson with creativity and innovation in bringing a course in feminism to the University.

Junior Erin Goundrey took that class with

Anderson. "He is the first man I ever encountered who was concerned with the women's movement and supported it fully."

Others remembered the professor for the "great life" he lived. "He lived an incredible life," said senior Clark Libbey, who defined his relationship with Anderson as friendship first, then student/professor.

"He lived all over the world-Africa, New Orleans, Libbey said. "I remember sitting on his front porch, listening to him tell stories about living in New Orleans, and going to listen to the jazz guys for a dollar. He lived life the way he wanted to...and he was very good at it.

Easton said he maintained regular contact with his ailing colleague, visiting him the day before he entered the coma. "He was always in good spirits," Easton said. "Always good."

"There was

always humorous banter between us," Easton remembered. When I visited him at the hospital and asked how he was doing, he'd reply, 'I'm surviving' and then laugh. And when I asked how the food was, he said, 'Well, it is hospital food."

As is the hallmark of a popular professor, Anderson will be remembered most for his treatment of students.

"He was my friend, professor and direction," said Libbey. "He was a great man."

articles.headline: Presidential Finalists Announced
articles.author: Dave Campbell
articles.body:
Ohio Wesleyan can expect it's new president by Feb. 5, according to Dick Fusch, acting Dean of Academic Affairs. After eight months of searching the Presidential Search Committee announced the three finalists at Monday night's faculty meeting.

The finalists are:
**Dr. Thomas B. Courtice, President of West Virginia Wesleyan College in Buchannon, West Virginia

**Dr Melvyn D. Schiavelli, Chancellor and Professor of Chemistry at the College of William and Mary in Williamsburg, Virginia.

** Dr. James S. Vinson, President and Professor of Physics at the University of Evansville in Evansville, Indiana.

According to a letter to the Ohio Wesleyan community from Helen C. Smith, chairperson of the presidential search committee, each of the candidates will be visiting campus within the next two weeks.

Dr. Courtice will be the first candidate to visit campus. He will be here Monday, Jan. 24. Dr. Schiavelli will visit campus Wednesday, Jan. 26, and Dr. Vinson will be here Thursday, Feb. 3.

Smith's letter said each candidate will be present at a reception in the Monnett Room of the Mowry Alumni Center for an open

reception from 5:15-6:00 each respective evening.

"All interested members of the campus community are invited to attend these receptions, "Smith said.

Response forms will be available to interested individuals to convey their "impressions and responses" of the candidates to the Presidents's Office before the committee makes their recommendation to the Board of Trustees.

Smith also said a copy of each candidate's full resume is available in the President's Office.

Also at the meeting Lou Szalontai, vice president ofbusiness affairs and treasurer, reported that "insufficient insulation" caused the water main breaks in the Hamilton Williams Building on Jan. 10 and 11 (see story page 4).

Szalontai said that the building will be fully operational as soon as possible.

New carpet, wallpaper, and

sheet rock has been ordered and the contractor is working diligently to get everything finished.

Dean Don Bishop reported that applications for next year's freshman class are downby 10 percent but the percentage of honors applications is up. Bishop said "the expected freshman class of 490 students is still feasible but at this time it's a little tenuous for people in my position"

The next open faculty meeting is Feb. 21 at 7:45 pmin Benes Room C.

articles.headline: Hartley Remembered, 'Champion Of People'
articles.author: David Erlewine and Catherine Ngubane
articles.body:
People who knew Trevor Hartley made it clear that he will be remembered for the life he lived, and not the way he died.

Hartley, 19, of 2975 Brandon Road, Upper Arlington, a suburb of Columbus, was a resident of 113 Thomson Hall.

A freshman, he played fullback for the Ohio Wesleyan football team. He played in all the junior varsity games and a couple of varsity games.

Michael Hollway, Ohio Wesleyan's football coach and Hartley's academic adviser, spoke at Hartley's funeral on Saturday, Jan. 15, at Union Cemetery in Columbus.

In his speech, Hollway said Hartley was an unselfish and amazing person, and a successful athlete.

Hollway added that people should not remember Trevor for his last act on earth.

Hartley's University professors also remembered his life.

"Because Trevor was in his first year we were just beginning to know him. In our department we look at incoming students and try to predict what kind of teacher they will be," Gary DeCoker, an assistant professor of education.

"We saw a gentle enthusiasm in his [Trevor] working with young children," added DeCoker. "In our classes he expressed his education ideals, as do most of our students."

DeCoker said Hartley wondered allowed whether he would be able to meet the daily challenges of teaching.

"It is a tragedy that we'll never be able to see him implement his ideals in a classroom," said DeCoker. "We will miss Trevor and the person Trevor wanted to become."

Akbar Mahdi, an assistant professor of sociology, said Hartley was not a top student in his class but was a good person.

Hartley was a freshman discovering life on campus and had a passion for sports, said Mahdi. "There was nothing about his behavior that would suggest that he was a troubled kid. I was really shocked when I heard the news of his death."

Mahdi said many students expressed deep sorrow and sympathy for what happened. "That in itself is heart-warming to know that so many people cared."

"This was his way of trying to make it a nicer world."

Jauffrineau said Trevor's father has shown everyone a lot of support.

Trevor's note to his father contained no blame or anger toward anyone, J. Hartley said. "Trevor said it was nota nice world and he was going to a better world and he would wait for me there."

Jauffrineau stressed that no one should be blamed. "One thing that's important to know is that we have proof that he planned this a long time ago. As far as we can tell, Trevor had this planned a year ago. Nothingthat might have recently happened is the cause of his death. He was determined, and he used the most lethal way to do it.... It wasn't a compulsive reaction he had. He knew exactly what he was doing. I don't want anyone to blame students or family members."

Heins agreed with Jauffrineau that evidence exists that Hartley had this planned up to a year ago. Both said the evidence is very personal and declined to talk about it.

"Trevor was my best friend here and soon-to-be roommate," Jauffrineau said. "Trevorhada a huge heartand he was really hurt by what was going on in the world. He's a lot happier where he is now."

Several firefighters put on uniforms and stood honor guard over the casket at the funeral, Cooper said. Hartley's body wastransported in a fire department medic vehicle, and several chiefs stood at guard outside as the vehicle drove by.

A memorial service was planned for Tuesday, Jan. 18, at 4 p.m. in Selby Stadium.

Michael Hollway, Hartley's adviser and football coach, could only ask why when he found out about Hartley's death. "It'sa contradiction to everything we knew about Trevor," he said.

"I'm divorced and I raised Trevor myself, "J.Hartley said, "and I've hada lot of guiltoverwhat happened. The counselors told me there's nothing I could have done. Trevor was the classic case of being able to hide it. The counselors told me he just decided to leave this world forabetterplace."

About 1600 people attended the funeral services Saturday, Jauffrineau said. "That shows how many people Trevor was close with."

"It shows how many people he touched," Heins said.

Hartley's football teammates spoke about his enthusiasm and good nature.

Junior Jeff Worobel said Hartley was friendly and hard working. "It seemed like he had lots of friends."

Sophomore John Dotson agreed, "He was alwayshaving fun."

Robert Brandt, associate dean of students, said, "The University is very sad about Trevor's death. We embrace and loveallofour students."

Brandt said the Chaplin's office, the office of student services and the University Counseling Services are open to students who would like to share their feelings about Hartley's death.

Hartley went to Jones Intermediate School and graduated from Upper Arlington High School in 1993.

According to officials, Hartley remained in close contact with students, administration, and faculty at both schools.

Tim Reno, principal of Jones Intermediate, said Hartley went on trips with the Jones Intermediate ski club and helped students with their skiing.

"He was sort of a champion for anyone struggling," Reno said. "He took kids under his wing who were struggling and helped them. He did a lot with eighth gradersandmany ofthem lookedupto him.

The students partly looked up to Hartley because he was a football player, Reno said, but the other part was that he cared a lot about those kids that were struggling.

Pat Stewart, vice principal at Upper Arlington High School, said even though Hartley graduated last year he remained popular and involved at the high school.

"The thing that's the most heart-wrenching is that there are literally hundreds of people he could have contacted who would have been there-not just students, but adults."

Blaine Bierley, Hartley's guidance counselor at the high school, said Trevor was out-going, up-beat, friendly, and interested in people.

Bierley said a student told him yesterday about how on his first day of school Hartley was the first person to come up to him and welcome him and introduce himself.

"Hewasapeople person," Bierley said.

Karen Uretsky, a sophomore at Upper Arlington, said Hartley's suicide was hard to deal with because he was very popular and someone people looked upto.

"He was generally a very nice person and really treated everyone with respect," Uretsky said.

articles.headline: Dean Don Bishop Clarifies Statements
articles.author: Don Bishop
articles.body:
Dear Editor:

In the September 1 Transcript, an article about Ohio Wesleyan's freshman class contained a statement attributed to me that Kenyon, Denison, and Wittenberg had lowered their admission standards. I want to correct this error.

During the interview with the reporter I noted Ohio Wesleyan's overlap with these colleges as well as Wooster and Oberlin had increased in the number of students admitted to Ohio Wesleyan and one of these peer institutions. My point in citing this was to stress that more applicants to Ohio Wesleyan in the past five years have been of high or very good quality. I felt we deserved the credit and recognition for improving our applicant pool.

Unfortunately the reporter interpreted the information that more of our accepted students were gaining admission to Denison, Kenyon and Wittenberg as meaning those three schools had lowered their admission standards and accepted students which had traditionally been turned down for admission.

It is important for our students at Ohio Wesleyan who read the September article to know that Denison, Kenyon, and Wittenberg have indeed been successful and they have maintained their selectivity. They have not lowered their selectivity. The point of the cross applicant admit data was to establish Ohio Wesleyan's positive growth. There had been speculation that the smaller class size implied the University was less successful in comparison to our peer Ohio colleges. This was not true and the cross applicant admit rates were simply meant to clarify Ohio Wesleyan's situation.

The implication in the article that we are much more selective than the schools is also incorrect. Last year the 1992 freshman class profiles at Denison and Wittenberg were very similar to Ohio Wesleyan's and Kenyon's profile was higher.

It is important to me that our campus community notes this correction. I truly regret the articles. negative comments about Wittenberg, Denison, and Kenyon were based on an interview with me. The topic of cross applicant admit data is rather technical and not easy to understand. I should have been more careful in my conversation to explain it. I also should have corrected this error earlier.

This fall have been a hectic semester of admission travel and I regret that I did now write about these corrections earlier.

Sincerely,

Don Bishop

articles.headline: Campus Center Springs a Leak
articles.author: Catherine Ngubane
articles.body:
Insufficient insulation of water pipes reportedly caused the flooding of the Hamilton-Williams Campus Center Monday, Jan. 10, and early inthe morning of Tuesday, Jan. 11, said Sharon Cramer, acting director of physical plant and superintendent of maintenance and operations.

Cramer said on Monday at 1 p.ma2 1/2-inch high pressure water pipe that feeds the sprinkler system broke causing the University to close the building for Tuesday and Wednesday.

The break was in the Pritchard Conference Room, room 304, next to the chaplain's office.

Public Safety estimated 35,000- 40,000 gallons of water poured from the pipebefore water was shutoffto the entire building.

Because of safety regulations, the pipes to the sprinkler system had to be refilled when the leak was repaired, but an additional pipe broke at 2 a.m. Tuesday morning.

This leak was not discovered forthree hours due to the time it occurred, and Public Safety estimated another 30,000-35,000 gallons of water spilled in the Campus Center before the spill was stopped.

This break occurred opposite the first one, on the other sideofthechaplain's office.

Cramer said an investigation of the breakage is in progress to determine who is liable for the damage and what can be done to prevent a similar problem in future.

She would not comment onthe details of the meetings already held with the architects and the contractors.

She indicated that there are some options on how to prevent the pipes from breaking again but added, "Until I am certain of what is going to happen, I cannot say anything because it will create too much controversy." She said further details will be available today.

In the Jan. 11 issue of The Delaware Gazette, Cramer said she suspected cold weathermay have contributedtothelinebreaks.

"We're still concerned that it doesn't happenagain, with cold weather" this week, said Todd Wilson, Ohio Wesleyan director of news and information.

Don Chenoweth, dean of student activities told members of the Wesleyan Council on Student Affairs (WCSA) that the problem will be fixed by insulation ofthe pipes.

He said, "We are finding out more information about the building." For example, the building is unevenly heated.

"We hope to have thebuilding looking normal in a few weeks," said Chenoweth.

"Liability has not yet been ascertained, but the insurance will pay to repair thebuilding and the University has a $20,000-$25,0000 deductible that it will have to cover," he added.

"I am not certain about this, but what usually happens in such cases is that the insurance company pays forthe damages and then it has to go after the liable people to get its money back," said Chenoweth.

articles.headline: Students Complain Area In Smith Lot Is Unclearly Marked
articles.author: Tricia Labuda
articles.body:
While public safety cites students for blocking a fire exit in the parking lot of Smith Hall East, student judicial courts suspend most fines because students say the lot markings are ambiguous.

Justice Irfan Nooruddin said, "In this court, all [related] cases are dismissed, and all the other courts have pretty much followed that." He said the students said the area is not clearly marked. They also say that there are no lines and no sign, and citations are issued inconsistently.

Freshman Andy D'Antoni said he received a ticket when he parked three car widths away from the oval concrete fixture that public safety says indicates a fire lane.

"The space was not marked," he said. "There was no concrete parking marker, but there were two or three spaces left, so I pulled into the one closest to the concrete [markers]."

He said he appealed the fine and it was suspended. He said the court told him they would try to get the fire lane clearly marked.

Donald Chenoweth, dean of student services, said "a yellow line [around the oval fixture] is pretty clear. He said additional marking is unnecessary. "To make everything perfectly clear everywhere would require a lot of signs. We cannot rely on having signs everywhere to control and regulate our behavior.

Sophomore Amy Fletcher said she received a parking ticket the first week of school when she parked between two cars in a space near the concrete island.

"When you see people parking there all the time," she said, "you assume that it is a legal place to park. She said her ticket was suspended.

Chenoweth said some students could park there and not get tickets but, he said, that does not justify others parking there. All parking enforcement is uneven," he said. "It is impossible to be consistent unless we have continual enforcement present, which is not feasible."

Nooruddin, a sophomore, said the courts wrote a memo around late October and gave it to Residential Life to relay to public safety.

"We made a recommendation to the University to put a sign up, to clearly mark the spot with a cornerstone, and to have public safety enforce the policy on a consistent basis," he said.

Fred Moyer, chief of public safety, said the issue has been a problem since the lot was expanded three years ago. He added, "I think it [the marking] is as plain as day myself."

A public safety officer estimated that between 35 and 50 tickets have been given this year concerning this spot.

Moyer replied to the judicial board around November 15. He said he sent accompanying pictures and said the questionable area is a driveway. "If it was meant for parking, we would have parking blocks the whole way across, he said.

Moyer said the concrete divider provides for one entry and one separate exit into the second part of the parking lot. He said the area just south of the concrete island and north of the last parking block, which is the side most frequently filled, is for entering the parking lot.

He said this side is wider than the area north of the island so fire trucks can make the turn, not so students can have more parking.

Moyer said if the lot were paved, they would have painted yellow stripes to indicate no parking. Because it is not, he said, "If I can find something over break to further clarify the no-parking area, I will put it up."

articles.headline: Distinguished Alum Dies On Christmas Eve
articles.author: Catherine Ngubane
articles.body:
At 65, the champion of "The Power Of Positive Thinking," and 1920 Ohio Wesleyan University graduate, Rev. Norman Vincent Peale died in Pawling, New York, on Dec. 24.

"Peale was one of the University's well known and beloved graduates," said Todd Wilson, director of public relations.

Wilson added, "At the time of his death, Peale was a life trustee of OWU. He was named a life trustee in 1984. He had been a trustee from 1952 to 1958 and was always a good friend and contributor to the University, said Wilson.

"He contributed $200,000 towards the building of the Hamilton-Williams Campus Center where the Norman Vincent Peale Chapel is located," added Wilson.

The University awarded Peale with the Distinguished Achievement Citation, which is the highest honor the University bestows on its alumni that have made significant contributions in their fields and humanity. One to two people are honored with the award per year, said Wilson.

Peale had written and spoken extensively on the power of positive thinking.

According to Wilson, Peale recognized the importance of positive thinking at the University. "One advertisement in fortune magazine stated that Peale found the power of positive thinking at a liberal arts institution," he added.

"He spoke to tens of millions of ordinary people around the world through his book The Power of Positive Thinking, an all-time inspirational best seller, with nearly 230 million copies sold in 41 languages," according to the Columbus Dispatch of Sunday, Dec. 26.

However not every one agreed on his message and the means of disseminating it. "He was accused of establishing a cult of reassurance, practicing ritualistic incantation as a form of psuedopsychiatry, making too much money and vulgarizing religion," according to the Dispatch article.

Peale was a Dutch Reformed Minister for 50 years and his writings included A Guide To Confident Living and You Can Win.

According to documents, Peale wrote for a weekly column entitled "Confident Living," which appeared on weekends in over 80 metropolitan newspapers. He was also an Editor-in-Chief of Guideposts, an inspirational magazine with over 225,000 subscribers.

He was the 1992 commencement speaker at Ohio Wesleyan, said Wilson. When introducing Peale as the speaker, former University President David Warren referred to him as, "The century's most influential Protestant clergyman."

Peale died in Dutchess County on his 20-acre farm after suffering a stroke in December.

He is survived by his wife Ruth Peale, two daughters: Margaret Everett and Elizabeth Allen and a son John Peale, said Wilson.

images.caption: The late Norman Vincent Peale shown here with his wife, Ruth Peale, spoke at commencement in 1992.

articles.headline: T-shirt Vendors Kicked Off Campus
articles.author: Seth G. Daniel
articles.body:
Joe College, Inc., a T-shirt company, was asked by University administrators to leave the Hamilton-Williams Campus Center seven weeks ago for selling T-shirts that were inappropriate, according to Don Chenoweth, dean of student services.

"I think they were offensive, said Chenoweth. "In this case, the T-shirts violated our community values. They glorified alcohol consumption and degraded women."

Jeff Zeigler, director of Hamilton-Williams Campus Center and student activities, said he was the one who asked the vendors to leave. Zeigler said he was disappointed that students were sold the shirts. "We're a private institution and we work very hard to educate our students on what is proper," said Zeigler.

articles.headline: Phonathon Is Ringing In Big Money For OWU
articles.author: Monica Sarkar
articles.body:
Workers of Ohio Wesleyan's phonathon have raised $412,000 of their $500,000 goal this semester.

Jill Gaby, assistant director of the annual fund, said the results of the drive have a tremendous effect on the school's budget. It's definitely crucial that we meet our annual fund goal," she said.

The annual fund supports scholarships, financial aid, general educational maintenance costs, and faculty and administrative salaries, said Gaby. The goal of the annual fund drive is $2.4 million, of which the phonathon is one of many fund raisers.

The phonathon employs 40 students. The purpose of the program is to call parents, alumni, and friends of the University for financial help, said Gaby. Callers can also inform people of current events at Ohio Wesleyan. "Gifts range from $5 to $2000, said Gaby.

Junior supervisor Jennifer Birkmeyer started as a caller her freshman year. It's really fun to go in and make a lot of money for the University," she said. "One night we brought in $60,000. The callers enjoy a good night."

Freshman Marci Love said she started working for the phonathon because her roommates told her about it.

"I love doing it because it's really great talking to alumni. All of them are really successful so it gives me a positive outlook. Also, they've stayed in touch with people they went to school with, which is encouraging.

Birkmeyer said she enjoys talking to the older alumni. "If we get people who went here 40 years ago, they tell stories about the dorms that we live in. It's really neat to hear their stories.

Gaby said callers will focus next semester on people who have never given, past students parents, and people who haven't given in awhile. They will call Sunday through Thursday from 6-9 p.m.

"Even though we only have $88,000 left to raise, it won't be as easy as it sounds," she said. "However, we have a great bunch of students that are energetic and motivated to reach the goal."

did not act as a censor in asking the vendors to leave. "It would be a far reach to consider it a free speech issue," he said.

It had little to do with student freedom said Chenoweth. He said with this issue you have to think of the University as a business owner and the issue a business matter.

Freshman Taylor Haley, a salesman for Joe College, Inc., said he believed the University was acting as a censor for the students. He said the way the University handled the issue was wrong.

"I think if you asked any student, they wouldn't find anything offending about them [the shirts]," said Haley.

Freshman Michael Shore said he believed the University should not have asked the vendors to leave. "The students were buying the shirts in order to wear them, and if the University doesn't have a dress code, then there shouldn't be a code for saying what is appropriate and inappropriate to sell."

Freshman Charles Baker said it appeared to be an act of censorship, but the University handled the issue the right way.

Chenoweth described one of the inappropriate shirts as having a double meaning. He said it advertised a bar that had drinks in the front and poker in the rear.

Haley said the shirts being sold were Big Johnson T-shirts and co-ed naked sports T-shirts. "They were things that kids wear every day," he said.

With the course content and the types of lectures Ohio Wesleyan has having T-shirts that are degrading to women are things we shouldn't have here," said Chenoweth.

According to Chenoweth the University has never asked a vendor to leave in the past.

articles.headline: Dance team seeks opportunity to perform at basketball games
articles.author: Carmelita R. Casey
articles.body:
"In Living Color's fly-girl dancing" was how one member of Ohio Wesleyan's new dance team described the type of jazz dance being performed by the five women of the Bishop Beat.

The members currently perform at the women's home basketball games and plan to pursue competition some time next year. They have already performed at two games and for the Red and Black Revue.

The purpose is to bring more spirit into basketball," said captain Callie Morrison, a sophomore. "I'd like to see more girls involved, mainly to have fun; it's an outlet of energy."

Although all the members share a love for dance, none of them are dance minors. Morrison and the co-captain, junior Tegan Craig, both said they got involved with the Beat partly because Ohio Wesleyan does not offer a major in dance.

"I've been dancing since I was four years old," said Craig. "The dance program here is modern; I wasn't used to that. I'ma triple major, so I have a lot of stress, and dancing helps me relieve that stress," she said.

Morrison said the Beat has had some trouble acquiring status because they are not considered an actual group until they have six members. Until that time they also cannot get funding from WCSA.

"We got practice space in Edgar Hall in the 4th floor dance studio but we could get booted if Orchesis needs it," Morrison said.

Like most other college dance teams, the Bishop Beat would like to perform during the men's basketball games but were told they could not do so by the advisor of the cheerleading squad.

"I personally do not think there should be any conflict between the cheerleaders and the dance team," said Craig.

"I've been kind of offended that they haven't gotten in touch with me," Boggs said. "It [the dance team] takes weight off the cheerleading squad to do everything; I'm very open to the idea."

On the other hand, senior cheerleader Beth Marshall said she could see how some cheerleaders might be defensive to the idea of sharing time with the dance team.

"We're [the cheerleaders] not even taken as a sport, and then you have something else taking away from you," Marshall said.

Craig said despite the fact that the Bishop Beat members are not performing at the men's basketball games, she is content with supporting the women's games.

"There are two to three games a week, I'm pretty happy with it," Craig said. "I think even if there wasn't a

Senior Kim Boggs, captain of the crowd I'd still dance."

articles.headline: Women cagers on four-game streak
articles.author: Chris Masters
articles.body:
It took a lot longer than many had expected, but the Ohio Wesleyan women's basketball team has pieced together a four-game winning streak, and has begun a charge at the NCAC title.

The Bishops entered Wednesday night's game with Oberlin, having split four games over the Christmas holidays. Ohio Wesleyan dropped games at Baldwin-Wallace and Denison, before rebounding to defeat Case Western Reserve at home and Thomas More by two on the road.

"We used the time over the break very effectively," Ohio Wesleyan coach Nan Carney-DeBord said. "It will pay off in the difficult games to come."

However, in the course of this tough stretch, the Bishops lost leading scorer Cindy Bailey to a foot injury. According to team trainer Tom Agne, Bailey has a sprained arch and will be out for at least another week.

"It's not healing like we'd hoped," Agne said. "It needs more therapy and her schedule doesn't really allow for that."

"Cindy isapartofthisteam," Carney-DeBord said. "She'll contribute when she comesback."

In the interim, Carney-DeBord has plugged sophomore Dena Greene in the starting lineup. In her first start against Thomas More, Greene poured in a career-high 14 points in leading the Bishopsto the 66-64win.

Against Oberlin, there would not be such a narrow margin of victory. The Yeowomen cameto Branch Rickey Arena winless on the season and it showed. After Oberlin tied the score at two, Ohio Wesleyan reeled off 21 straight points. The Bishops opened up a comfortable 52-11 halftime lead and cruised in with an 87-23 thrashing of Oberlin (0-10,0-6).

"We just needed to focus on us (as a team)," Bishop assistant coach Laura Bumpsaid.

Junior Teri Hamlin led the way with 12 points, and Greeneadded 10 points, on five-for-five shooting from the field. All 14 Bishops dented the scoring column. Freshman Angie Quatman came off the bench to notch seven points and 12 rebounds.

"Our younger players are rising to the occasion," Carney-DeBord said. "A lot of different players are stepping up and playing well."

For Oberlin, center Dee Wells had six points, 11 rebounds and 10blocked shots, allteam-highs. The latter mark was also a new NCAC record, smashing the old mark of seven held by four different players.

Ohio Wesleyan traveled to Wooster Saturday afternoon for another conference clash, this time with the Lady Scots. Wooster was a dismal 1-5 in the NCAC this season, and the Bishops weren't about to fall victim to an upset.

Hamlin scored 15 points, and senior post Kierstan Grunow snatched 10 rebounds as Ohio Wesleyan defeated the Lady Scots 65-48. The Bishops survived a 27 percent shooting performance in the second half by hitting 140ftheir free throws in the period. Greene added 10 points in her third straight start.

Ohio Wesleyan (7-4,5-2) hasa difficult stretch ahead ifit plans to contend for the NCAC championship. The Bishops travel to Richmond, Ind. tonight to battle the NCAC's leading scorer, Shannon Ferguson, and the Earlham Quakers. Saturday afternoon, Ohio Wesleyan goes to Meadville, Pa. for a 1:00 tilt with Allegheny. Both games are considered important heading into a pivotal game a week from today against the NCAC leader Wittenberg at Branch Rickey Arena.

articles.headline: Bishop hoopsters down Wooster
articles.author: Kevin Henderson
articles.body:
The Ohio Wesleyan men's basketball team has come alive since the Christmas break. The Bishops lengthened their winning streak to six games last week by defeating NCAC opponents from Oberlin and Wooster.

The Bishops simply seem to beplaying more cohesively since the holidays, due in part to the time they had to remain on campus for practice and games while the rest of the University returned home to their families. But the extra time spent is paying off and now that senior Bob Croft is on top of his game once again, Ohio Wesleyan is looking more and more confident as it heads into the second half of conference play this week.

The Bishops traveled to Oberlin Wednesday evening to take on the Yeomen and cameaway with a convincing 79-60 victory. Junior Rod Mitchell was a near-perfect six of seven from the field, two of two from behind the three-point line, and two oftwo from the free throw line for a team-high 16 points. Junior Bo Dobbs chipped in with 14 rebounds. Junior Justun Lott and senior Ryan Spicer were boththree of five from three-point range in the victory, which raised Ohio Wesleyan's conference record to 4-2.

The Bishops tested their skills and new found shooting accuracy against a more proven foe, the Wooster Scots (10-4,4-2). The Bishops and Scots entered Saturday night's matchup at Branch Rickey Arena tied for third place in the conference behind Wittenberg and Kenyon.

The Bishopscame prepared as Croft led the team with 15 points and six rebounds and the defense allowed Wooster just one field goal over the final six minutes. Ohio Wesleyan took sole possession ofthird place with a 62-50 win. Athalftime, the Bishops led 25-18, but they quickly lengthened the lead to 18 early in the second half. The Bishops shot 17 for 21 from the free throw line in the second halfto stifle a late Wooster run.

The Bishops' improved shooting overallis added proof that their shortened break was well worth it. Their shooting percentage has risen dramatically, as evidenced by a 63% figure in the second halfofthe Wooster game.

Allthings look positive for the Bishops (9-5,5-2) asthey head into tonight's contest against Earlhamat home. The addition of shooting forward J.R. Shumate, the sophomore transfer from Otterbein, has strengthened the bench play, as well as hopes for another NCAC title.

Following the Earlham game, Ohio Wesleyan will embark on a four-game road trip. The first contest is Saturday afternoon at3:15 in Meadville, Pa. against Allegheny. A week from today, the Bishops will get anothercrack at the top team in the NCAC, Wittenberg, in Springfield. Tipoffforthat game is set for 7:30p.m.

articles.headline: Students Should Attend Presidential Candidate Receptions
articles.author: Bob West
articles.body:
Ohio Wesleyan sure has seen better days than the last couple of weeks, hasn't it? Just take a look at the front page of this paper for evidence of Wesleyan's recent hardship. Trevor Hartley's suicide came as a shock, as would any college student taking his own life. The Hamilton-Williams Campus Center mess immediately inconvenienced everybody on this campus. The recent death of alumni Norman Vincent Peale (20) was noted across the country. And all at the same time the University is nearing the selection of a president to lead Ohio Wesleyan into the twenty-first century.

The past, the present and the future of Ohio Wesleyan have all come crashing together is a jumbled, soaking wet heap.

It would be easy here to harp on the negatives and to warn everyone of the impending doom of the University. I used this space for similar messages before. Looking pessimistically to the past however, will benefit no one. It's time for a lesson in Norman Vincent Peale 101--the power of positive thinking. I have written of lacking student activism on this campus before. I have also seen the potential for change from the students though, too. Students can ultimately be an influence, if they choose to, and the best place to start is the top.

Ohio Wesleyan is a fine university, but one where the students have many concerns and complaints. The opportunity to voice our concerns is now. The three finalists for University president have been announced- -Dr. Thomas B. Courtice, Dr. Melvyn D. Schiavelli and Dr. James S. Vinson. All three gentlemen will be visiting campus within the next two weeks, and they will be present at open receptions for students to meet and question them. The students will have the opportunity to voice concerns about Ohio Wesleyan to our next leader.

Sophomores and juniors want to live off-campus soon? Talk about it at the receptions! Freshman don't want to eat this same quality of food for the next three years? Go to the receptions! Greeks concerned with their role on campus? WCSA want more recognition as a governing body? Minorities unhappy with the University's current attitudes towards equality? Go to the receptions!! Find out what these candidates positions are, and lead a charge of student voices for the best candidate. I hear the complaints. I know most of you have them. Go to these receptions. They're being held in the Monnett Room of the Mowry Alumni Center because the University isn't expecting a great turnout. Prove them wrong! Bring along concerned friends, strength lies in numbers. Use your WCSA class representatives (remember them?) or go with your entire group who has a concern--but no matter what--GO! Let's make sure the next president of Ohio Wesleyan knows the students will be a loud voice on this campus. Or else the complaints should be swallowed for quite some time.

articles.headline: Confidential Message To OWU ServiceMaster Intercepted
articles.author: Dorothy Chen
articles.body: STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL. Memo. From: Headquarters, ServiceMaster, Milwaukee, WI To: ServiceMaster manager, Ohio Wesleyan University, Delaware, OH Re: Implementing additional food system policies. Dear Mr. Block, In the organizational meeting at ServiceMaster Headquarters on 7/27, the committee carefully considered the ServiceMaster outlet under your supervision. We understand that you and your management committee have made the commendable moves of increasing food prices, and preventing the transfer of food points. The Headquarters Committee has made a few additional suggestions which we felt might help strengthen the food service system. They are as follows: a) The committee observed that the eating process will run more smoothly if students do not have to stop by the counters in the dining halls to collect utensils and spices before they eat. Therefore, we strongly suggest that all eating utensils such as forks, knives, and spoons be removed from each dining facility. Ketchup, mayonnaise, mustard, paper napkins, and straws should also be removed. All these items should be provided by the students themselves, and will be available at the Thomson Grocery Store for convenient purchase. Removing all items from counters will not only prevent the daily hassle of stopping by these counters, but will also facilitate the easy flow of traffic from the food areas to the tables. b) During peak hours, students often have to wait to get seats, which severely agitates them or prevents them from getting a meal at all. Therefore, we suggest that students be limited to a ten-minute dining period during the rush period. This will allows more students to purchase food items. Perhaps several automated clocks with musical alarms could be set on each table to inform students that their eating time periods are at an end. c) The committee has observed that the availability of suggestion cards often excites students to write derogatory comments. Furthermore, the replies of the management to the students' suggestions seldom seem to satisfy students, serving only to agitate them even further. In view of this, we feel that suggestion cards (which were introduced by the former food service) be removed. d) It has been observed that students are often confused if they have too great a variety of food to choose from. The student, whose chief priority lies in the academic field, should not be forced to make difficult choices where food is concerned. Thus, we suggest that you limit the variety of the food served. For instance, Colorado University's dining facilities have "potato extravaganza nights exciting events where potatoes cooked in many different styles are served. Furthermore, cutting down on food variety will reduce expenses, and lighten the burden of the cooks. e) Finally, we feel that a reduction in the salaries of workers should be carried out. This has a two-fold purpose: it will encourage workers who are already unhappy to leave, and it will strengthen the bond between management and the workers who have decided to stay. Workers who leave can be easily replaced by members of the non-working force. Workers who stay will understand that they too can be easily replaced, and this will increase their dependability on the management. Thus, a stronger relationship will evolve between staff and management. These policies should be implemented immediately.

articles.headline: Fraternity Encourages Frosh To Think Greek
articles.author: Mark Steffey '96, Jason McGrath '97
articles.body:
Attention Freshman Males:

Well, it's that time of year again. The time for the Ohio Wesleyan campus to take a few weeks and THINK GREEK. This is the time that freshman men on campus love. Free food, parties. hockey games. A trip to The I fill in mid-January is a real treat for those interested in fraternity life. While the norm is hostile fraternity brothers and stubbornness in distribution of alcohol, Rush Week brings fraternity brothers that are all smiles and an abundance of free beer. And in the end it's all for the sake of brotherhood, right?

As many of you may or may not know, there is one fraternity that will not be involved in Kush Week. That brotherhood is Alpha Sigma Phi Alpha Sigma Phi defies the norm when it comes to fraternities here at Ohio Wesleyan.

How so? Here are some facts you probably aren't aware of

1. Oflast year seight male Mortar Board members (the junior honorary society), four were members of Alpha Sigma Phi.

2. The President and three voting members of WCSA are members of Alpha Sigma Phi.

3. The Editor-in-Chief of this publication is a member of Alpha Sigma Phi

4. The cumulative grade point average of the membership of Alpha Sigma Phi is about 3.3, the highest among Greek organizations and higher than the independent average.

5. Alpha Sigma Phi teams won both the soccer and volleyball intramural championships this fall

6. Recently, a national organization filmed a How to Rush video featuring the members of the Epsilon Chapter of Alpha Sigma Phi here at Ohio Weslevan."

All of these facts work to set Alpha Sigma Phi apart from any other fraternity in that they show the unique character of the individuals that make up the brotherhood. It is easily seen when you look at the membership that these are well-rounded guys with moral standards that are unique among Greek men here on campus.

This week make the most of what is offered on The Hill. If you find a fraternity that suits you, where you could spend the next three years of your life--go for it. But if you don't. if it all seems like a facade and the smiles seem a bit forced, know that there is a higher standard. and that standard is the brotherhood of Alpha Sigma Phi Think about it.

articles.headline: The Government Might Have Better Success Regulating Mother Nature
articles.author: George F. Will
articles.body:
One hundred and thirty Julys ago the president, referring to the Mississippi, said, "The father of waters again goes unvexed to the sea. Lincoln was pleased, the occasion being the triumph of the siege of Vicksburg by a general from the Mississippi River town of Galena, Ill.: U.S. Grant.

It would be nice if that willful river--today 16 miles wide on some Illinois and Missouri plain--would be more vexed by human ingenuity. But the big river, by riveting our attention on the unpredictable and uncontrollable sphere of life (which is almost all of life), has some lessons for the river town in which the national government sits. Mother Nature along the Mississippi and human nature along the Potomac are both misbehaving.

The Mississippi runs through American's imagination. On it Huck Finn found freedom by floating away from chafing facets of civilization. And in 1901, in a house on a Mississippi River bluff near Little Falls, Minn., a boy was born whose early impulses for solitary adventuring were indulged on the great river--young Charles Lindbergh in his canoe.

For a long time now people have been trying to tame the river. Today, while deeply regretting the material damage and mourning the human tragedies the river is causing, it is difficult to suppress a secret exhilaration about the way the river casually shrugs off the restraining hand of man. We need recurring reminders of how little mastery our species has-- of itself, of events, of nature, of the present or the future.

Regarding nature, at least, we have come some way toward caution about what we can know and do. Not long ago serious people felt that manipulating nature was a practical possibility. For example, in his "Eisenhower: The President, Stephen Ambrose recounts a June 1957 meeting that Eisenhower held with three scientists concerning peaceful uses of atomic energy. Physicist Edward Teller, perhaps hoping that Eisenhower's interest in such uses might make Eisenhower support additional atomic detonations for test purposes, suggested the possible use of atomic devices for altering the flow of rivers and even to modify the weather by changing the dust content of the air.

Such technological hubris has a jarring, even childlike, ring today. Who nowadays would try to interest a president in attempting to control the climate? Well, come to think about it, the vice president might.

By some strange law of the physics of intellectual life, an intellectual excess in one direction is apt to produce a comparable and opposite excess. So today we hear much from people (today's vice president, for example) who believe that climate, and much of the rest of the natural world, is highly changeable, even fragile. They believe that human behavior, unless controlled by wise government, will have large and lasting deleterious consequences- -global warming, or cooling, or whatever. And they believe that well-regulated societies can regulate the planet's thermostat, and much else.

The technological bravado of the 1950s and the apocalyptic environmentalism of the 1990s are cousins. It is difficult to decide which is potentially more harmful, and it is wrong to say that they are really very different. Both assume that it is easy to discombobulate, either consciously or carelessly, the planet's fundamental processes.

However, the greening of the blasted slopes of Mount St. Helens testifies to the planet's often underestimated resiliency. In contrast, we consistently overestimate the ability of our governance to subdue social events, which always are at floodtide. Consider two current matters. one abroad, one domestic.

U.S. forces went to Somalia eight months ago for a few weeks-a few months, at most--to facilitate food distribution. Now U.S. gunships have used missiles and cannon to blast something called the command center" of someone identified as a fugitive Somali warlord." Anumber of somali civilians were killed and wounded, and an enraged Somali mob killed four journalists who came to the scene to assess the damage. As our "nationbuilding progresses. political levees presumably will be built to control the flow of such passions.

Meanwhile, back along the Potomac, some members of the gargantuan House-Senate conference on the $500 billion five-year deficit reduction package say the final package may actually have $20 billion less in deficit reductions. Oh

Still, it is awesome that these people have such mastery of economic projections and manipulations. They can, they say. anticipate the consequences of their legislative decisions on hundreds of millions of people making trillions of economic decisions over five years. Hence, they know precisely how much deficit reduction they are enacting, down to the last $20 billion over five years or $4 billion per year. which is one-quarter of one percent of the annual gross domestic product.

With such fine-tuning, they must have that Mississippi of red ink tamed Like the river.

enriched_ads.body:
Customer Service Representative

The Huntington National Bank of Delaware is looking for a qualified applicant to fill a part-time Customer Service Representative position. The hours are Monday, Wednesday and Friday, 1 p.m.-5:30 p.m. and Saturday, 8:30 a.m.-12:30 p.m. The selected candidate will be responsible for rendering legendary customer service while processing cash and non-cash transactions and cross-selling and explaining bank products and services. Applicants should possess excellent customer service and communication skills and have the ability to handle cash transactions and to utilize required sales techniques.

Huntington offers an excellent starting salary and a comprehensive benefits package which includes medical and dental insurance, paid life insurance, tuition reimbursement, stock plan and discounted rates on many bank services. We maintain a smoke-free environment and require pre-employment drug screening. Please apply in person between the hours of 9 a.m.- 1 p.m. Monday-Friday at:

41 S. High Street, 3rd Floor
or
7575 Huntington Park Drive

Huntington Operations Center
